title: Market Participants Survey results - April 2026
summary: The Bank of England's April 2026 Market Participants Survey (77 respondents, fielded 15-17 April) shows market participants expect the Bank Rate to remain at 3.75% through September 2026 before a gradual decline toward 3.00-3.25% by end-2027. The survey captured market views on factors driving a 76 basis point rise in UK short rates since the Middle East conflict onset, with respondents attributing 37.9% of the move to direct energy cost impacts. CPI inflation expectations center around 3.0-3.4% through 2026, moderating to 2.0-2.5% over longer horizons.
key_points: Median Bank Rate expectation holds at 3.75% through September 2026 MPC meetings, then shifts to 3.50% at November 2026 and 3.25% by March 2027
For April 30, 2026 MPC: 89.0% probability assigned to 3.75%, 9.8% to 4.00%. For June 2026: 67.6% probability of 3.75%, 24.7% of 4.00%
UK short rates increased 76 basis points since February 27 due to Middle East conflict; 37.9% attributed to direct energy cost impacts, 20.3% to second-round wage/price effects
Neutral rate estimate (neither expansionary nor contractionary): median 3.25% with interquartile range 3.00%-3.50%
CPI inflation median forecast: 3.0% end-2026 Q2, 3.4% end-2026 Q4, declining to 2.0% three years ahead
2026 GDP growth median expectation: 0.80%; long-run potential growth: 1.40%
why_it_matters: This survey provides the Bank of England's formal intelligence gathering on market expectations, offering policymakers insight into how rates markets are pricing the path of UK monetary policy. For market participants, the probability distributions around Bank Rate outcomes and the factor attributions for recent short rate moves offer a structured view of consensus positioning ahead of MPC meetings.
macro_context: The survey shows markets pricing a gradual easing cycle from 3.75% beginning late 2026, with CPI expected to remain above the 2% target through 2027. The market pricing incorporates significant uncertainty, with end-2026 Bank Rate outcomes spanning a wide distribution from below 3.00% to above 4.50%. The Middle East conflict was identified as the primary driver of the recent short rate repricing, with energy cost pass-through as the dominant factor.
